What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Conclusion
Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Unlike cell phones that fail when you need them most, a properly operated VHF radio connects you to rescue services, other boaters, and essential information anywhere your boat can reach. The skills covered in this guide, from basic operation to emergency procedures, become automatic with practice.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

[Excerpt 3 — VHFProtocolsUS.txt / vhfprotocolsus]
After you have made contact and communicated your needs, you are free to set sail as you were.

How To Make An Urgent Or Emergency Call On Marine VHF Radio
Distress or emergency calls made on marine VHF radios can change the predicament that you may find yourself in for the better or worse.

Follow the steps below to ensure that your call gets heard, understood, and responded to in time:

1️⃣ Identify the type of emergency you are in. Will you be using “Mayday,” “Securité,” or “pan-pan”? These terms are clarified in the table further down.

2️⃣ Tune your radio to channel 16

3️⃣ Repeat your signal three times. (e.g., ” Mayday. Mayday. Mayday”)

4️⃣ Next, follow with “This is” once, and your vessel name repeated three times.

5️⃣ State your position or location

6️⃣ State what kind of situation you are in (e.g., sinking)

7️⃣ Clarify how many people are on board the vessel and also if any require medical attention

8️⃣ Specify the kind of assistance you would need.

9️⃣ Say “over” once you are done communicating your requirements, but stay near the radio for as long as possible.

🚨 Example of a distress call: “Mayday! Mayday! Mayday! This is The Black Pearl, The Black Pearl, The Black Pearl. I am 5 miles east of Davy Jones’ Locker. We are sinking. Seven people are on board. Over.”

What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Conclusion
Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Unlike cell phones that fail when you need them most, a properly operated VHF radio connects you to rescue services, other boaters, and essential information anywhere your boat can reach. The skills covered in this guide, from basic operation to emergency procedures, become automatic with practice.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

Never test your radio by calling MAYDAY or transmitting on Channel 16 unnecessarily. Use Channel 9 for radio checks. In some areas, automated radio check systems exist on Channel 9, 24, 27, or 28 depending on your location. These systems record your transmission and play it back so you hear how you sound. Alternatively, arrange with a boating friend to test radios on a working channel. The Coast Guard also permits brief radio checks on Channel 16 during periods of low activity, but use this sparingly and keep it brief.

[Excerpt 3 — CompleteGuideVHF.txt / 13	Bridge-to-bridge	Navigation, bridges, locks, commercial traffic]
Start by testing your radio without causing false alarms. Tune to Channel 9 and call for a radio check: “This is [vessel name], requesting a radio check on Channel 9, over.” If another boater hears you, they will respond confirming your transmission quality. Some areas have automated radio check systems that respond with a recorded message. Listen for responses and note how clearly your transmission comes through. Practice this at your dock or anchorage before you actually need to rely on the radio offshore.

The radio spectrum worldwide is governed by the International Radio Regulations. In the UK the associated legislation is the Wireless Telegraphy (WT) Act 2006 (as amended). These regulations stipulate the licences that are required both for the radio installation and the radio operator. Although maritime (ship) radio’s primary function is to ensure safety of life at sea, the international radio regulations permit the use of ship radio on inland waterways as well as at sea. The rules for the installation and use of radio (e.g. VHF) apply equally when the equipment is used inland.

[Excerpt 3 — CompleteGuideVHF.txt / completeguidevhf]
Your cell phone might feel like a lifeline on land, but the moment you leave the dock, it becomes nearly useless. I learned this the hard way during my first offshore trip when I discovered my smartphone had zero bars just three miles from shore. That is when I realized why every experienced boater treats their marine VHF radio as essential safety equipment, not an optional gadget.

Learning how to use a marine VHF radio properly is one of the most important skills any boater can develop. Unlike cell phones that depend on towers, VHF radios work anywhere on the water through simple line-of-sight communication. They connect you directly to the Coast Guard, nearby vessels, marinas, and bridge operators. Channel 16 serves as the universal emergency and hailing frequency, monitored 24/7 by rescue authorities across the country.

In this guide, I will walk you through everything you need to know to operate a marine VHF radio with confidence. We will cover basic operation for beginners, understand why Channel 16 matters so much, learn proper hailing procedures, and master emergency protocols that could save lives. Whether you are new to boating or just want to brush up your radio skills, this guide has you covered.

What Is a Marine VHF Radio?
A marine VHF radio is a two-way communication device designed specifically for watercraft. VHF stands for Very High Frequency, and these radios operate between 156 and 162 megahertz on designated marine channels. Unlike cell phones that require expensive infrastructure and monthly subscriptions, VHF radios use free public airwaves that work instantly with the push of a button.

How VHF Communication Works?
Marine VHF radios use simplex communication, meaning transmissions travel one direction at a time. When you press the Push-to-Talk button, you transmit. When you release it, you receive. This is different from phone conversations where both parties speak simultaneously. The radio waves travel in a straight line, giving them a range of roughly 20 miles depending on antenna height and conditions.

The higher your antenna, the farther your signal travels. A fixed-mount radio with an antenna mounted 15 feet above the waterline can typically reach 15 to 20 miles to another vessel or shore station. Handheld units with their antennas just a few feet above water level usually work reliably within 3 to 5 miles of shore.

Question: Why is it important to test my radio before going offshore?

To confirm the transmission quality of your radio before needing it in critical situations. Channel 9 is designated for non-commercial communication and radio checks.. Automated radio check systems may provide recorded responses in some areas..

Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

How to Hail Another Vessel or Marina in 2026?
Hailing is the process of making initial contact with another station. Doing it properly shows you understand radio etiquette and gets you a faster response. Many new boaters feel nervous about their first hails, but following a simple script makes the process straightforward.

The Standard Hailing Protocol
Start by tuning to Channel 16. Listen briefly to ensure the channel is not in use. Then press your PTT button and say the name of the station you are calling, followed by your own vessel name, then the word “over.” For example: “Marina Del Ray, Marina Del Ray, this is sailing vessel Windward, over.”

Wait 15 to 30 seconds for a response. If you do not hear anything, try again. If there is still no response after three attempts, the station may not be monitoring or may be out of range. Once the station responds, they will either answer your question immediately or suggest switching to a working channel for the conversation.

When using VHF radios for marine communication, finding a channel, tuning in, and starting a conversation is not straightforward.

What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Conclusion
Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Unlike cell phones that fail when you need them most, a properly operated VHF radio connects you to rescue services, other boaters, and essential information anywhere your boat can reach. The skills covered in this guide, from basic operation to emergency procedures, become automatic with practice.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

[Excerpt 1 — VHFPro.txt / Standard Marine Communication Phrases]
Professional VHF communication follows structured patterns that ensure message clarity while reducing transmission time and preventing channel congestion during busy maritime operations.

Essential communication elements include:
► Station identification: Clear vessel name and call sign identification
► Message markers: Instruction, advice, warning, information, question, answer, request, intention
► Standard responses: Affirmative and negative acknowledgments with full repetition
► Position reporting: Precise location using degrees, minutes, and geographic references
► Time references: UTC notation with clear hour and minute designations

Example (Initial Contact):

Vessel A: "Port Control, Port Control, this is MV Ocean Star, 
call sign Hotel Alpha Bravo Charlie One, on Channel One-Two. 
How do you read me? Over."

Port Control: "MV Ocean Star, this is Port Control. 
Reading you loud and clear. Go ahead. Over."

[SECTION BREAK]

Seven-Alpha 15 minutes later at One-Four-Zero-Zero local time? 
My position bearing One-Four-Zero degrees from Main Light, 
distance Five nautical miles. Over."

[Excerpt 2 — CompleteGuideVHF.txt / 13	Bridge-to-bridge	Navigation, bridges, locks, commercial traffic]
For example, to spell “FL 1234 AB” you would say: “Foxtrot Lima, one two three four, Alpha Bravo.” Using the phonetic alphabet shows professionalism and ensures clarity when reception is poor.

[Excerpt 3 — VHFProtocolsUS.txt / vhfprotocolsus]
Specific words, codes, phrases, and numbers must be utilized while talking on a marine VHF radio.

Speaking over the radio in your everyday vernacular will confuse people and will likely not be taken seriously. Furthermore, you could end up with a citation or a fine.

Specific Words To Use While Talking On A Marine VHF Radio:

Mayday: used for distress calls. Only to be used in grave and imminent danger.
Pan-pan: used for potentially dangerous situations but not yet at “mayday” level.
Securité: used to alert and bring attention to nearby boaters of something. Such as urgent marine information broadcasts.
Affirmative: used instead of “yes.”
Negative: used instead of “no.”
WILCO: used to say “will confirm.”
Roger: indicative of agreement and compliance
Over: indicates the end of the transmission message
Hear/ read/ copy: shows that your transmission has been heard
Stand by: end transmission, but continue to monitor channel
Repeat: repeat the last transmission
The NATO Alphabet And How To Use It On A Marine VHF Radio
When required to spell out something, the traditional ABCs you learned in school will be useless here.

At sea, the NATO alphabet is utilized with “I spell” prefacing the word. So, for example, if you were to spell out “whale,” the communication would go as follows: “I spell Whisky, Hotel, Alpha, Lima, Echo.”

The same applies to any letters of the alphabet that need to be relayed. “A” would be Alpha, “B” would be Bravo, and so on.

The Proper Way To Communicate Numbers Over Marine VHF Radio
The numerical system only goes from 0-9 in maritime communications. Therefore, numbers above 9 will be conveyed by first saying “figures” and then the individual numbers.

So if you wanted to say 35 (thirty-five), it would be said as “figures three five.”

1. Practice spelling your vessel name and registration numbers using the phonetic alphabet. 2. Record yourself and listen back. Outcome: Improved clarity in communication on the radio.

What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Conclusion
Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Unlike cell phones that fail when you need them most, a properly operated VHF radio connects you to rescue services, other boaters, and essential information anywhere your boat can reach. The skills covered in this guide, from basic operation to emergency procedures, become automatic with practice.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

[Excerpt 3 — CompleteGuideVHF.txt / 13	Bridge-to-bridge	Navigation, bridges, locks, commercial traffic]
Excessive static usually indicates improper squelch adjustment. Turn the squelch knob clockwise until the static just disappears. If static persists or you hear breaking voices, you may be receiving distant stations weakly. This is normal for VHF. If you hear engine noise through the radio, your power connections may need filtering. Ignition noise creates a specific ticking sound that increases with engine RPM. Installing noise filters on power leads often solves this.

[SECTION BREAK]

If other stations report your signal is weak or you cannot reach stations you previously heard, check your antenna connections. Corroded connections at the antenna base are the most common range killers. Inspect the antenna for physical damage. Antennas do degrade over time, typically lasting 5 to 10 years depending on exposure to sun and salt. If using a handheld, remember that 1 watt of power has inherently limited range. For offshore work, you need a 25-watt fixed mount with a quality external antenna mounted as high as practical.

Question: how do I troubleshoot a VHF radio that won't produce sound?

1. check the volume control. 2. adjust the squelch knob counterclockwise. 3. check external speaker connections. 4. verify functionality of handheld radio speakers. Outcome: radio produces static indicating it is operational.

What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Conclusion
Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Unlike cell phones that fail when you need them most, a properly operated VHF radio connects you to rescue services, other boaters, and essential information anywhere your boat can reach. The skills covered in this guide, from basic operation to emergency procedures, become automatic with practice.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. What channels should you use for regular conversations? Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

How to Hail Another Vessel or Marina in 2026?
Hailing is the process of making initial contact with another station. Doing it properly shows you understand radio etiquette and gets you a faster response. Many new boaters feel nervous about their first hails, but following a simple script makes the process straightforward.

The Standard Hailing Protocol
Start by tuning to Channel 16. Listen briefly to ensure the channel is not in use. Then press your PTT button and say the name of the station you are calling, followed by your own vessel name, then the word “over.” For example: “Marina Del Ray, Marina Del Ray, this is sailing vessel Windward, over.”

Wait 15 to 30 seconds for a response. If you do not hear anything, try again. If there is still no response after three attempts, the station may not be monitoring or may be out of range. Once the station responds, they will either answer your question immediately or suggest switching to a working channel for the conversation.

Question: How do I properly hail another vessel on Channel 16?

1. Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. 2. Call the other station's name twice, identify yourself, and say over. 3. Switch to a working channel after initial contact. 4. What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

Harmonised examination procedures for the General Operator's Certificate and Restricted Operator's Certificate were introduced for maritime radio 1 operators performing radiocommunication duties on board vessels subject to SOLAS. Likewise harmonised examination procedures for the Short Range Certificate and Long Range Certificate were introduced for maritime radio operators performing radiocommunication duties on board NON – SOLAS vessels. Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

[Excerpt 2 — CompleteGuideVHF.txt / 13	Bridge-to-bridge	Navigation, bridges, locks, commercial traffic]
What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Conclusion
Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Unlike cell phones that fail when you need them most, a properly operated VHF radio connects you to rescue services, other boaters, and essential information anywhere your boat can reach. The skills covered in this guide, from basic operation to emergency procedures, become automatic with practice.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

If there is no DSC acknowledgement after a short interval (5 minutes) then, if you are able to offer assistance, acknowledge by voice on Channel 16: “Mayday “Name of vessel sending the distress message, followed by their call sign or MMSI “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]; Call sign or MMSI of your vessel “Received mayday “State what assistance you can give [including estimated time of arrival (ETA) if proceeding to the casualty] “Over” You should use any available means to relay the distress message to an appropriate coast station. Urgency If you are concerned about the safety of a person or vessel, you can send an urgency announcement using a DSC All Ships Urgency Call, nominating a working channel. Tune to Channel 16 to make the urgency call: “Pan pan, pan pan, pan pan “All stations – say 3 times. “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times] “Call sign or other identification “MMSI of own vessel “Please go to Channel [nominated working channel] “Out” Tune to the working channel and send your urgency message. Safety To pass safety information to HM Coastguard (HMCG) use an Individual DSC call with safety priority if available on your radio, entering the appropriate MMSI number. Transmit the DSC call and wait for the Coastguard acknowledgement. Accept the acknowledgement and ensure your radio is on the working channel indicated in the response. You should wait for the Coastguard to contact you on that channel. If your radio does not support the call, then you should make a voice call on Channel 16.

What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Conclusion
Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Unlike cell phones that fail when you need them most, a properly operated VHF radio connects you to rescue services, other boaters, and essential information anywhere your boat can reach. The skills covered in this guide, from basic operation to emergency procedures, become automatic with practice.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

MAYDAY signals grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. Use MAYDAY when lives are threatened, a vessel is sinking, someone has a medical emergency, or fire is out of control. MAYDAY calls get absolute priority on the radio.

Recommendation proposed by the Working Group “Frequency Management” (FM) Original text of the Recommendation adopted by the "European Radiocommunications Committee" (ERC): INTRODUCTION The full implementation of the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS) has made it necessary to review and to harmonise the examination requirements for the certificates of maritime radio operators. Harmonised examination procedures for the General Operator's Certificate and Restricted Operator's Certificate were introduced for maritime radio 1 operators performing radiocommunication duties on board vessels subject to SOLAS. Likewise harmonised examination procedures for the Short Range Certificate and Long Range Certificate were introduced for maritime radio operators performing radiocommunication duties on board NON – SOLAS vessels. The GMDSS was fully implemented as per 1. February 1999. Because of the decision-making by WRC 07, the DSC and radio telephone procedures were amalgamated into one set of regulation (see RR Article 32). MAYDAY signals grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. Use MAYDAY when lives are threatened, a vessel is sinking, someone has a medical emergency, or fire is out of control. MAYDAY calls get absolute priority on the radio.

Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

The Standard Marine Communication Phrases (SMCP) has been compiled: - to assist in the greater safety of navigation and of the conduct of the ship, - to standardize the language used in communication for navigation at sea, in port-approaches, in waterways, harbours and on board vessels with multilingual crews, and - to assist maritime training institutions in meeting the objectives mentioned above. These  phrases are not intended to supplant or contradict the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972 or special local rules or recommendations made by IMO concerning ships' routeing, neither are they intended to supersede the International Code of Signals, and when applied in ship’s external communication this has to be done in strict compliance with the relevant radiotelephone procedures as set out in the ITU Radio Regulations. Furthermore, the SMCP, as a collection of individual phrases, should not be regarded as any kind of technical manual providing operational instructions. The SMCP meets the requirements of the STCW Convention, 1978, as revised, and of the SOLAS Convention, 1974, as revised, regarding verbal communications; moreover, the phrases  cover the relevant communication safety aspects laid down in these Conventions. Use of the SMCP should be made as often as possible in preference to other wording of similar meaning; as a minimum requirement users should adhere as closely as possible to their wording in relevant situations. In this way they are intended to become an acceptable safety language, using English  for the verbal interchange of intelligence among individuals of all maritime nations on the many and varied occasions when precise meanings and translations are in doubt, increasingly evident under modern conditions at sea. The accompanying CD/Cassette is designed to familarize users with the pronunciation of the phrases.

[Excerpt 2 — IMO standard marine comms phrases.pdf / NAV 46/WP.3]
FOREWORD As navigational and safety communications from ship to shore and vice versa, ship to ship , and on board ships  must be precise, simple and unambiguous, so as to avoid confusion and error, there is a need to standardize the language used. This is of particular importance in the light of the increasing number of internationally trading vessels with crews speaking many different languages since problems of communication may cause misunderstandings leading to dangers to the vessel, the people on board and the environment. In 1973 the IMO Maritime Safety Committee agreed at its twenty-seventh session that, where language difficulties arise, a common language should be used for navigational purposes and that language should be English. In consequence the Standard Marine Navigational Vocabulary (SMNV) was developed, adopted in 1977 and amended in 1985. In 1992 the IMO Maritime Safety Committee at its sixtieth session instructed the IMO Sub- Committee on Safety of Navigation to develop a more comprehensive standardized safety language than the SMNV, 1985, taking into account the changing conditions in modern seafaring and covering all major safety-related verbal communications. At its sixty-eighth session in 1997 the IMO Maritime Safety Committee adopted the Draft Standard Marine Communication Phrases (SMCP) developed by the IMO Sub-Committee on Safety of Navigation. The Draft SMCP, following international trials, was amended at the forty- sixth session of this Sub-Committee and final consideration given at the IMO Maritime Safety Committee at its [... ] session  in the light of remarks received by the Organization. Under the International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers, 1978, as revised 1995, the ability to understand and use the SMCP is required for the certification of officers in charge of a navigational watch on ships of 500 gross tonnage or more.

The SMCP does not intend to provide a comprehensive Maritime English syllabus which is expected to cover a far wider range of language skills to be achieved in the fields of vocabulary, grammar, discourse abilities, etc., than the SMCP could ever manage.. However,  PART A in particular,  should be an indispensable part of any curriculum which is designed to meet the corresponding requirements of the STCW Convention, 1978, as revised. In addition, PART B offers a rich choice of situations covered by vention, 1978, as revised, phrases well suited to meet the communication requirements of the STCW Con which are implicitly expected to be satisfied  by mariners. The SMCP should be taught and learnt selectively, according to the users` specific needs rather than completely. The respective instruction should be based on practice in the maritime environment and be implemented through appropriate modern language teaching methods.

[SECTION BREAK]

The SMCP builds on a basic knowledge of the English language. It was drafted on purpose in a simplified version of Maritime English to reduce  grammatical, lexical and idiomatic varieties to a tolerable minimum, using standardized  structures for the sake of its function aspects, i.e. diminishing misunderstanding in safety related verbal communications, thereby endeavouring to reflect present Maritime English language usage on board vessels and in ship-to-shore/ship-to- ship communications. This means, in phrases offered for use in emergency and other situations developing under considerable pressure of time or psychological stress as wells as in navigational warnings, a block language was applied which sparingly uses, or frequently  omits, the function words the, a/an, is/are as done in seafaring practice. Users, however, may  be flexible in this respect. Further  communicative features may be summarized as follows: - avoiding synonyms - avoiding contracted forms - providing fully worded answers to "yes/no"-questions and basic alternative answers to sentence questions - providing one phrase for one event, and - structuring the corresponding phrases after the principle: identical invariable plus variable.

PART B calls attention to other on-board standard safety-related phrases which, supplementary to PART A, may also be regarded useful  for Maritime English instruction.

[Excerpt 1 — BoatUS.txt / 3 Tips for Using a VHF Radio]
In an emergency, your broadcast needs to be more structured. With the radio tuned to Channel 16 and the power set to high, begin your broadcast by stating either "Mayday" or "Pan-pan" three times over. Mayday is used when you're in a life-threatening situation. Pan-pan is the appropriate call to make when you're in a bad situation that isn't life threatening at the moment but could become life threatening. Next, state your vessel's name, latitude and longitude, a brief description of your boat, and the nature of your emergency. Speak slowly and clearly, and wait for a response from the Coast Guard. Once the Coast Guard knows the exact situation and location, be ready for some follow-up questions. You're likely to be asked about such things as the size and type of the boat you're on, the number and age of the people on board, and whether anyone has any medical training, if it's applicable to the situation.

Tip
Listen to make sure that the channel is clear before transmitting.
Even if you don't get an answer, continue making the emergency broadcast with those first three vital bits of information. The authorities (or perhaps a nearby pleasure boater) may be listening, even if you can't hear them calling back. Usually the best way to make sure your vital info gets through with no confusion or mistakes is to ensure that you have digital selective calling (DSC) active on your radio. This requires a Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number and a link to your GPS, unless you've got a newer VHF with a built-in GPS. When you press the DSC "panic button" on the VHF, the radio will automatically transmit your vessel information and exact location. And since it's digitally processed and uses narrow receiver bandwidth, it also boosts range over normal voice communications.

If you know for a fact that you haven't activated DSC, check out the article "Setting Up A VHF Radio With Digital Selective Calling", which tells you how to integrate your VHF and GPS. Then visit the MMSI website (free for members) to get an MMSI number and register your radio.

Think of VHF communications like the highways and byways of our nation. They're public, everyone uses them, and everyone benefits from them. But they can become clogged with overuse and unpleasant due to discourtesy. Follow the proper VHF protocol, and everyone will be in for a better boating experience — and a safer one, too.

MAYDAY signals grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. Use MAYDAY when lives are threatened, a vessel is sinking, someone has a medical emergency, or fire is out of control. MAYDAY calls get absolute priority on the radio.

To make a MAYDAY call, tune to Channel 16, set your radio to high power, and transmit: “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY. This is [vessel name], [vessel name], [vessel name].” Then provide your MMSI number if you have one, your position using latitude and longitude or bearing and distance from a known point, the nature of your distress, the kind of assistance you need, and the number of people on board.

Continue calling MAYDAY until you get a response. If you have a DSC-equipped radio, press the distress button to automatically alert the Coast Guard with your position and vessel information.

[Excerpt 3 — GMDSS VHF DSC procedures for small boat users - GOV.UK.pdf / Distress alert acknowledgement]
When a DSC radio receives a distress alert it will sound an audible alarm. Immediately cease any transmission that may interfere with distress traffic and continue a listening watch on Channel 16. If there is no DSC acknowledgement after a short interval (5 minutes) then, if you are able to offer assistance, acknowledge by voice on Channel 16: “Mayday “Name of vessel sending the distress message, followed by their call sign or MMSI “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]; Call sign or MMSI of your vessel “Received mayday “State what assistance you can give [including estimated time of arrival (ETA) if proceeding to the casualty] “Over” You should use any available means to relay the distress message to an appropriate coast station. Urgency If you are concerned about the safety of a person or vessel, you can send an urgency announcement using a DSC All Ships Urgency Call, nominating a working channel. Tune to Channel 16 to make the urgency call: “Pan pan, pan pan, pan pan “All stations – say 3 times. “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times] “Call sign or other identification “MMSI of own vessel “Please go to Channel [nominated working channel] “Out” Tune to the working channel and send your urgency message. Safety To pass safety information to HM Coastguard (HMCG) use an Individual DSC call with safety priority if available on your radio, entering the appropriate MMSI number. Transmit the DSC call and wait for the Coastguard acknowledgement. Accept the acknowledgement and ensure your radio is on the working channel indicated in the response. You should wait for the Coastguard to contact you on that channel. If your radio does not support the call, then you should make a voice call on Channel 16.

[Excerpt 3 — VHF-procedures-Scheldt-area-EN.md / VHF PROCEDURES]
- Traffic participants must indicate in good time if they wish to deviate from a route.
- During navigation assistance, the traffic controller gives an overview of the current traffic picture, possibly supplemented with calculated, expected situations, such as encounters and passages in (passing) distance and time.
- To convey the position of a moving ship, the position of the bow of the vessel relative to a point ahead in the fairway, or in bearing and distance, is used. For a stationary ship, this is the middle of the track or a radar echo.
- The **passing distance** is the distance that will exist during passing between the adjacent sides of two ships, or between a ship and an obstacle. The passing distance is only reliable provided the ground track remains constant.
- The **ground track** of a ship is its direction of movement relative to true north over the ground.
- The **distance between two vessels** is the measured shortest distance. For head-on traffic this is the bow-to-bow distance; for overtaking traffic this is the bow-to-stern distance.
- The **abeam distance** to a buoy, beacon or obstacle is the distance between the bow of a moving ship and an object, measured perpendicular to the direction of the fairway.
- The **distance to a navigation mark** is the shortest distance to that navigation mark.
- The terms **"opvarend" (upbound)** and **"afvarend" (downbound)** are used east of the Schone Waardin. In English these are "ingoing" and "outgoing".
- In the approach areas and the roadstead area, the terms **"inkomend" (inbound)** and **"uitgaand" (outbound)** are used, in English "inbound" and "outbound".
- To indicate a position before or beyond a certain point, we use **"bovenwaarts" (upstream)** or **"benedenwaarts" (downstream)**. In English these are "above" and "below".
- If the traffic controller must give information about a part of the area not covered by radar and for which no visual information is available, he or she will make this known to the traffic participant requesting the information.
- Position information is always given relative to known reference points. These points are visible, known and can be found on the nautical chart.
- A **bearing** between two known points is the horizontal angle relative to true north and the point being observed. The figures are spoken one by one.
- **Distances** are given to a tenth of a kilometre or a tenth of a nautical mile (also called a "cable"). Where confusion is possible, e.g. between the English numbers fifty and fifteen, the digits are spoken separately.
- Names of buoys and markers must not be translated. They are pronounced as they appear on the nautical chart. For example, W6 is pronounced "Whiskey 6".
- "Buoy transit" (doorwisselen van boeien) refers to two consecutive buoys marking a bend in a channel coming into line relative to the bow of the ship.
- Position reports can be given in two ways: using the along/across method, or via bearing and distance. The traffic controller may supplement this with ground track and ground speed. The intervals between reports depend on the traffic picture, the speeds of vessels, meteorological conditions, nautically critical points, and so on.
- An **along/across position report** comprises, on the one hand, the point to which the ship has progressed along the length of the fairway, and on the other hand, the distance of the ship in the transverse direction, measured to the locally customary reference line — for example the buoy line, the light line, the shore, etc. The transverse distance may also be expressed as 1/3 red, 1/3 green, or mid-channel. If the distance is less than 1/3 of the fairway width, the distance is expressed in metres to the buoy line.
  Measurements are always given relative to the starboard side (SB) of the vessel. If this is not possible because there is no reference, the traffic controller will explicitly state this.
- A **position report via bearing and distance** looks at the position of the forward part of the assisted ship in relation to a known point.
  Here too, the traffic controller may add ground track and ground speed. If the ship is sailing parallel to the reference line, moving away from it, or approaching it, this will be stated.
- If the traffic controller gives position reports (on request) while a ship is coming to anchor, he or she agrees which point the reports will be relative to. Either the planned anchor position is indicated — this may be an anchorage as shown on the chart, or a position chosen by the master or pilot. From the bow, the traffic controller gives information by bearing and distance (B/D) to the anchor position, including speed over ground. As a standard for reporting frequency, the following applies:
  - Distance more than 1500 m: B/D every 500 m
  - Distance 1500 to 500 m: B/D every 200 m
  - Distance 500 to 200 m: B/D every 100 m
  - From 200 m: B/D every 50 m.

For anchor watch purposes, the master or pilot must state the number of nautical miles and/or cables relative to a fixed point, and the number of shackles on deck.

Vessel Traffic Services provide navigation assistance, traffic organization, and information services that enhance maritime safety in designated areas. VTS communications follow standardized formats ensuring efficient information exchange between vessels and shore-based traffic control centers.

[Excerpt 2 — VHF-procedures-Scheldt-area-EN.md / VHF PROCEDURES]
A Vessel Traffic Service is a service implemented by the authorities that provides the means to communicate with shipping traffic and to respond to situations developing within the VTS area. The service increases the safety and efficiency of shipping and contributes to "Safety of Life at Sea" and to environmental protection.

A VTS is responsible for:

- **Providing timely and relevant information** about factors that may influence navigation and that support the on-board decision-making process.
  This includes, among other things, information on the position, identity and destination of other ships, and hydrological and meteorological information.

- **Monitoring and planning vessels** so as to contribute to the safe and smooth handling of shipping traffic.
  This involves providing essential, up-to-date and timely information to support the on-board navigational decision-making process. This support consists of providing timely information, advice and instructions. The information may relate to anything in the chain of operations, such as lock planning, tidal windows, the availability of pilotage services, and so on.

- **Providing timely and relevant information** to respond to the development of unsafe situations.
  Essential, up-to-date and timely information is provided to support the on-board navigational decision-making process. This support consists of providing timely information, advice and traffic instructions.

To achieve this, a VTS can provide information, warnings or traffic instructions where necessary.

Advanced distress alerting enables specification of emergency nature through pre-configured distress categories that provide rescue services with immediate situation awareness for appropriate response coordination.

Distress nature specification enhances rescue response effectiveness by providing specific emergency information that enables proper resource allocation and response planning before voice contact establishment.

Distress nature categories:
• Fire or Explosion - Shipboard fire emergencies requiring specialized response
• Flooding - Hull breach or water ingress threatening vessel safety
• Collision - Impact with other vessels, structures, or underwater obstacles
• Grounding - Vessel aground requiring assistance or rescue
• Listing - Dangerous heel indicating potential capsizing threat
• Sinking - Imminent vessel loss requiring immediate evacuation
• Disabled and Adrift - Loss of propulsion or steering capability
• Abandoning Ship - Crew evacuation in progress or planned
• Piracy Attack - Armed robbery or hijacking incident
• Man Overboard - Person in water requiring rescue assistance

Distress calls/messages have absolute priority over all other communications. When heard, all other transmissions should cease and a listening watch should be kept. Any distress call/message should be recorded in the ship’s log and passed to the master. On receipt of a distress message, if in the vicinity, immediately acknowledge receipt. If not in the vicinity, allow a short interval of time to elapse before acknowledging receipt of the message in order to permit ships nearer to the distress to do so.
