[Excerpt 1 — VHF-procedures-Scheldt-area-EN.md / VHF PROCEDURES]
- Traffic participants must indicate in good time if they wish to deviate from a route.
- During navigation assistance, the traffic controller gives an overview of the current traffic picture, possibly supplemented with calculated, expected situations, such as encounters and passages in (passing) distance and time.
- To convey the position of a moving ship, the position of the bow of the vessel relative to a point ahead in the fairway, or in bearing and distance, is used. For a stationary ship, this is the middle of the track or a radar echo.
- The **passing distance** is the distance that will exist during passing between the adjacent sides of two ships, or between a ship and an obstacle. The passing distance is only reliable provided the ground track remains constant.
- The **ground track** of a ship is its direction of movement relative to true north over the ground.
- The **distance between two vessels** is the measured shortest distance. For head-on traffic this is the bow-to-bow distance; for overtaking traffic this is the bow-to-stern distance.
- The **abeam distance** to a buoy, beacon or obstacle is the distance between the bow of a moving ship and an object, measured perpendicular to the direction of the fairway.
- The **distance to a navigation mark** is the shortest distance to that navigation mark.
- The terms **"opvarend" (upbound)** and **"afvarend" (downbound)** are used east of the Schone Waardin. In English these are "ingoing" and "outgoing".
- In the approach areas and the roadstead area, the terms **"inkomend" (inbound)** and **"uitgaand" (outbound)** are used, in English "inbound" and "outbound".
- To indicate a position before or beyond a certain point, we use **"bovenwaarts" (upstream)** or **"benedenwaarts" (downstream)**. In English these are "above" and "below".
- If the traffic controller must give information about a part of the area not covered by radar and for which no visual information is available, he or she will make this known to the traffic participant requesting the information.
- Position information is always given relative to known reference points. These points are visible, known and can be found on the nautical chart.
- A **bearing** between two known points is the horizontal angle relative to true north and the point being observed. The figures are spoken one by one.
- **Distances** are given to a tenth of a kilometre or a tenth of a nautical mile (also called a "cable"). Where confusion is possible, e.g. between the English numbers fifty and fifteen, the digits are spoken separately.
- Names of buoys and markers must not be translated. They are pronounced as they appear on the nautical chart. For example, W6 is pronounced "Whiskey 6".
- "Buoy transit" (doorwisselen van boeien) refers to two consecutive buoys marking a bend in a channel coming into line relative to the bow of the ship.
- Position reports can be given in two ways: using the along/across method, or via bearing and distance. The traffic controller may supplement this with ground track and ground speed. The intervals between reports depend on the traffic picture, the speeds of vessels, meteorological conditions, nautically critical points, and so on.
- An **along/across position report** comprises, on the one hand, the point to which the ship has progressed along the length of the fairway, and on the other hand, the distance of the ship in the transverse direction, measured to the locally customary reference line — for example the buoy line, the light line, the shore, etc. The transverse distance may also be expressed as 1/3 red, 1/3 green, or mid-channel. If the distance is less than 1/3 of the fairway width, the distance is expressed in metres to the buoy line.
  Measurements are always given relative to the starboard side (SB) of the vessel. If this is not possible because there is no reference, the traffic controller will explicitly state this.
- A **position report via bearing and distance** looks at the position of the forward part of the assisted ship in relation to a known point.
  Here too, the traffic controller may add ground track and ground speed. If the ship is sailing parallel to the reference line, moving away from it, or approaching it, this will be stated.
- If the traffic controller gives position reports (on request) while a ship is coming to anchor, he or she agrees which point the reports will be relative to. Either the planned anchor position is indicated — this may be an anchorage as shown on the chart, or a position chosen by the master or pilot. From the bow, the traffic controller gives information by bearing and distance (B/D) to the anchor position, including speed over ground. As a standard for reporting frequency, the following applies:
  - Distance more than 1500 m: B/D every 500 m
  - Distance 1500 to 500 m: B/D every 200 m
  - Distance 500 to 200 m: B/D every 100 m
  - From 200 m: B/D every 50 m.

For anchor watch purposes, the master or pilot must state the number of nautical miles and/or cables relative to a fixed point, and the number of shackles on deck.

In an emergency, your broadcast needs to be more structured. With the radio tuned to Channel 16 and the power set to high, begin your broadcast by stating either "Mayday" or "Pan-pan" three times over. Mayday is used when you're in a life-threatening situation. Pan-pan is the appropriate call to make when you're in a bad situation that isn't life threatening at the moment but could become life threatening. Next, state your vessel's name, latitude and longitude, a brief description of your boat, and the nature of your emergency. Speak slowly and clearly, and wait for a response from the Coast Guard. Once the Coast Guard knows the exact situation and location, be ready for some follow-up questions. You're likely to be asked about such things as the size and type of the boat you're on, the number and age of the people on board, and whether anyone has any medical training, if it's applicable to the situation.

Tip
Listen to make sure that the channel is clear before transmitting.
Even if you don't get an answer, continue making the emergency broadcast with those first three vital bits of information. The authorities (or perhaps a nearby pleasure boater) may be listening, even if you can't hear them calling back. Usually the best way to make sure your vital info gets through with no confusion or mistakes is to ensure that you have digital selective calling (DSC) active on your radio. This requires a Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number and a link to your GPS, unless you've got a newer VHF with a built-in GPS. When you press the DSC "panic button" on the VHF, the radio will automatically transmit your vessel information and exact location. And since it's digitally processed and uses narrow receiver bandwidth, it also boosts range over normal voice communications.

If you know for a fact that you haven't activated DSC, check out the article "Setting Up A VHF Radio With Digital Selective Calling", which tells you how to integrate your VHF and GPS. Then visit the MMSI website (free for members) to get an MMSI number and register your radio.

Think of VHF communications like the highways and byways of our nation. They're public, everyone uses them, and everyone benefits from them. But they can become clogged with overuse and unpleasant due to discourtesy. Follow the proper VHF protocol, and everyone will be in for a better boating experience — and a safer one, too.

Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

[Excerpt 3 — CompleteGuideVHF.txt / 13	Bridge-to-bridge	Navigation, bridges, locks, commercial traffic]
What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Conclusion
Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Unlike cell phones that fail when you need them most, a properly operated VHF radio connects you to rescue services, other boaters, and essential information anywhere your boat can reach. The skills covered in this guide, from basic operation to emergency procedures, become automatic with practice.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

When a DSC radio receives a distress alert it will sound an audible alarm. Immediately cease any transmission that may interfere with distress traffic and continue a listening watch on Channel 16. If there is no DSC acknowledgement after a short interval (5 minutes) then, if you are able to offer assistance, acknowledge by voice on Channel 16: “Mayday “Name of vessel sending the distress message, followed by their call sign or MMSI “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]; Call sign or MMSI of your vessel “Received mayday “State what assistance you can give [including estimated time of arrival (ETA) if proceeding to the casualty] “Over” You should use any available means to relay the distress message to an appropriate coast station. Urgency If you are concerned about the safety of a person or vessel, you can send an urgency announcement using a DSC All Ships Urgency Call, nominating a working channel. Tune to Channel 16 to make the urgency call: “Pan pan, pan pan, pan pan “All stations – say 3 times. “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times] “Call sign or other identification “MMSI of own vessel “Please go to Channel [nominated working channel] “Out” Tune to the working channel and send your urgency message. Safety To pass safety information to HM Coastguard (HMCG) use an Individual DSC call with safety priority if available on your radio, entering the appropriate MMSI number. Transmit the DSC call and wait for the Coastguard acknowledgement. Accept the acknowledgement and ensure your radio is on the working channel indicated in the response. You should wait for the Coastguard to contact you on that channel. If your radio does not support the call, then you should make a voice call on Channel 16.

Distress calls/messages have absolute priority over all other communications. When heard, all other transmissions should cease and a listening watch should be kept. Any distress call/message should be recorded in the ship’s log and passed to the master. On receipt of a distress message, if in the vicinity, immediately acknowledge receipt. If not in the vicinity, allow a short interval of time to elapse before acknowledging receipt of the message in order to permit ships nearer to the distress to do so.

Some areas have automated radio check systems that respond with a recorded message. Listen for responses and note how clearly your transmission comes through. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

[Excerpt 2 — GMDSS VHF DSC procedures for small boat users - GOV.UK.pdf / Distress alert acknowledgement]
When a DSC radio receives a distress alert it will sound an audible alarm. Immediately cease any transmission that may interfere with distress traffic and continue a listening watch on Channel 16. If there is no DSC acknowledgement after a short interval (5 minutes) then, if you are able to offer assistance, acknowledge by voice on Channel 16: “Mayday “Name of vessel sending the distress message, followed by their call sign or MMSI “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]; Call sign or MMSI of your vessel “Received mayday “State what assistance you can give [including estimated time of arrival (ETA) if proceeding to the casualty] “Over” You should use any available means to relay the distress message to an appropriate coast station. Urgency If you are concerned about the safety of a person or vessel, you can send an urgency announcement using a DSC All Ships Urgency Call, nominating a working channel. Tune to Channel 16 to make the urgency call: “Pan pan, pan pan, pan pan “All stations – say 3 times. “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times] “Call sign or other identification “MMSI of own vessel “Please go to Channel [nominated working channel] “Out” Tune to the working channel and send your urgency message. Safety To pass safety information to HM Coastguard (HMCG) use an Individual DSC call with safety priority if available on your radio, entering the appropriate MMSI number. Transmit the DSC call and wait for the Coastguard acknowledgement. Accept the acknowledgement and ensure your radio is on the working channel indicated in the response. You should wait for the Coastguard to contact you on that channel. If your radio does not support the call, then you should make a voice call on Channel 16.

MAYDAY signals grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. Use MAYDAY when lives are threatened, a vessel is sinking, someone has a medical emergency, or fire is out of control. MAYDAY calls get absolute priority on the radio.

To make a MAYDAY call, tune to Channel 16, set your radio to high power, and transmit: “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY. This is [vessel name], [vessel name], [vessel name].” Then provide your MMSI number if you have one, your position using latitude and longitude or bearing and distance from a known point, the nature of your distress, the kind of assistance you need, and the number of people on board.

Continue calling MAYDAY until you get a response. If you have a DSC-equipped radio, press the distress button to automatically alert the Coast Guard with your position and vessel information.

[Excerpt 2 — GMDSS VHF DSC procedures for small boat users - GOV.UK.pdf / Distress alert acknowledgement]
When a DSC radio receives a distress alert it will sound an audible alarm. Immediately cease any transmission that may interfere with distress traffic and continue a listening watch on Channel 16. If there is no DSC acknowledgement after a short interval (5 minutes) then, if you are able to offer assistance, acknowledge by voice on Channel 16: “Mayday “Name of vessel sending the distress message, followed by their call sign or MMSI “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]; Call sign or MMSI of your vessel “Received mayday “State what assistance you can give [including estimated time of arrival (ETA) if proceeding to the casualty] “Over” You should use any available means to relay the distress message to an appropriate coast station. Urgency If you are concerned about the safety of a person or vessel, you can send an urgency announcement using a DSC All Ships Urgency Call, nominating a working channel. Tune to Channel 16 to make the urgency call: “Pan pan, pan pan, pan pan “All stations – say 3 times. “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times] “Call sign or other identification “MMSI of own vessel “Please go to Channel [nominated working channel] “Out” Tune to the working channel and send your urgency message. Safety To pass safety information to HM Coastguard (HMCG) use an Individual DSC call with safety priority if available on your radio, entering the appropriate MMSI number. Transmit the DSC call and wait for the Coastguard acknowledgement. Accept the acknowledgement and ensure your radio is on the working channel indicated in the response. You should wait for the Coastguard to contact you on that channel. If your radio does not support the call, then you should make a voice call on Channel 16.

Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

How to Hail Another Vessel or Marina in 2026?
Hailing is the process of making initial contact with another station. Doing it properly shows you understand radio etiquette and gets you a faster response. Many new boaters feel nervous about their first hails, but following a simple script makes the process straightforward.

The Standard Hailing Protocol
Start by tuning to Channel 16. Listen briefly to ensure the channel is not in use. Then press your PTT button and say the name of the station you are calling, followed by your own vessel name, then the word “over.” For example: “Marina Del Ray, Marina Del Ray, this is sailing vessel Windward, over.”

Wait 15 to 30 seconds for a response. If you do not hear anything, try again. If there is still no response after three attempts, the station may not be monitoring or may be out of range. Once the station responds, they will either answer your question immediately or suggest switching to a working channel for the conversation.

How to Hail Another Vessel or Marina in 2026?
Hailing is the process of making initial contact with another station. Doing it properly shows you understand radio etiquette and gets you a faster response. Many new boaters feel nervous about their first hails, but following a simple script makes the process straightforward.

The Standard Hailing Protocol
Start by tuning to Channel 16. Listen briefly to ensure the channel is not in use. Then press your PTT button and say the name of the station you are calling, followed by your own vessel name, then the word “over.” For example: “Marina Del Ray, Marina Del Ray, this is sailing vessel Windward, over.”

Wait 15 to 30 seconds for a response. If you do not hear anything, try again. If there is still no response after three attempts, the station may not be monitoring or may be out of range. Once the station responds, they will either answer your question immediately or suggest switching to a working channel for the conversation.

MAYDAY signals grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. Use MAYDAY when lives are threatened, a vessel is sinking, someone has a medical emergency, or fire is out of control. MAYDAY calls get absolute priority on the radio.

To make a MAYDAY call, tune to Channel 16, set your radio to high power, and transmit: “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY. This is [vessel name], [vessel name], [vessel name].” Then provide your MMSI number if you have one, your position using latitude and longitude or bearing and distance from a known point, the nature of your distress, the kind of assistance you need, and the number of people on board.

Continue calling MAYDAY until you get a response. If you have a DSC-equipped radio, press the distress button to automatically alert the Coast Guard with your position and vessel information.

[Excerpt 2 — BoatUS.txt / 3 Tips for Using a VHF Radio]
In an emergency, your broadcast needs to be more structured. With the radio tuned to Channel 16 and the power set to high, begin your broadcast by stating either "Mayday" or "Pan-pan" three times over. Mayday is used when you're in a life-threatening situation. Pan-pan is the appropriate call to make when you're in a bad situation that isn't life threatening at the moment but could become life threatening. Next, state your vessel's name, latitude and longitude, a brief description of your boat, and the nature of your emergency. Speak slowly and clearly, and wait for a response from the Coast Guard. Once the Coast Guard knows the exact situation and location, be ready for some follow-up questions. You're likely to be asked about such things as the size and type of the boat you're on, the number and age of the people on board, and whether anyone has any medical training, if it's applicable to the situation.

Tip
Listen to make sure that the channel is clear before transmitting.
Even if you don't get an answer, continue making the emergency broadcast with those first three vital bits of information. The authorities (or perhaps a nearby pleasure boater) may be listening, even if you can't hear them calling back. Usually the best way to make sure your vital info gets through with no confusion or mistakes is to ensure that you have digital selective calling (DSC) active on your radio. This requires a Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number and a link to your GPS, unless you've got a newer VHF with a built-in GPS. When you press the DSC "panic button" on the VHF, the radio will automatically transmit your vessel information and exact location. And since it's digitally processed and uses narrow receiver bandwidth, it also boosts range over normal voice communications.

If you know for a fact that you haven't activated DSC, check out the article "Setting Up A VHF Radio With Digital Selective Calling", which tells you how to integrate your VHF and GPS. Then visit the MMSI website (free for members) to get an MMSI number and register your radio.

Think of VHF communications like the highways and byways of our nation. They're public, everyone uses them, and everyone benefits from them. But they can become clogged with overuse and unpleasant due to discourtesy. Follow the proper VHF protocol, and everyone will be in for a better boating experience — and a safer one, too.

[Excerpt 3 — GMDSS VHF DSC procedures for small boat users - GOV.UK.pdf / Distress alert acknowledgement]
When a DSC radio receives a distress alert it will sound an audible alarm. Immediately cease any transmission that may interfere with distress traffic and continue a listening watch on Channel 16. If there is no DSC acknowledgement after a short interval (5 minutes) then, if you are able to offer assistance, acknowledge by voice on Channel 16: “Mayday “Name of vessel sending the distress message, followed by their call sign or MMSI “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]; Call sign or MMSI of your vessel “Received mayday “State what assistance you can give [including estimated time of arrival (ETA) if proceeding to the casualty] “Over” You should use any available means to relay the distress message to an appropriate coast station. Urgency If you are concerned about the safety of a person or vessel, you can send an urgency announcement using a DSC All Ships Urgency Call, nominating a working channel. Tune to Channel 16 to make the urgency call: “Pan pan, pan pan, pan pan “All stations – say 3 times. “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times] “Call sign or other identification “MMSI of own vessel “Please go to Channel [nominated working channel] “Out” Tune to the working channel and send your urgency message. Safety To pass safety information to HM Coastguard (HMCG) use an Individual DSC call with safety priority if available on your radio, entering the appropriate MMSI number. Transmit the DSC call and wait for the Coastguard acknowledgement. Accept the acknowledgement and ensure your radio is on the working channel indicated in the response. You should wait for the Coastguard to contact you on that channel. If your radio does not support the call, then you should make a voice call on Channel 16.

[Excerpt 1 — BoatUS.txt / 3 Tips for Using a VHF Radio]
In an emergency, your broadcast needs to be more structured. With the radio tuned to Channel 16 and the power set to high, begin your broadcast by stating either "Mayday" or "Pan-pan" three times over. Mayday is used when you're in a life-threatening situation. Pan-pan is the appropriate call to make when you're in a bad situation that isn't life threatening at the moment but could become life threatening. Next, state your vessel's name, latitude and longitude, a brief description of your boat, and the nature of your emergency. Speak slowly and clearly, and wait for a response from the Coast Guard. Once the Coast Guard knows the exact situation and location, be ready for some follow-up questions. You're likely to be asked about such things as the size and type of the boat you're on, the number and age of the people on board, and whether anyone has any medical training, if it's applicable to the situation.

Tip
Listen to make sure that the channel is clear before transmitting.
Even if you don't get an answer, continue making the emergency broadcast with those first three vital bits of information. The authorities (or perhaps a nearby pleasure boater) may be listening, even if you can't hear them calling back. Usually the best way to make sure your vital info gets through with no confusion or mistakes is to ensure that you have digital selective calling (DSC) active on your radio. This requires a Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number and a link to your GPS, unless you've got a newer VHF with a built-in GPS. When you press the DSC "panic button" on the VHF, the radio will automatically transmit your vessel information and exact location. And since it's digitally processed and uses narrow receiver bandwidth, it also boosts range over normal voice communications.

If you know for a fact that you haven't activated DSC, check out the article "Setting Up A VHF Radio With Digital Selective Calling", which tells you how to integrate your VHF and GPS. Then visit the MMSI website (free for members) to get an MMSI number and register your radio.

Think of VHF communications like the highways and byways of our nation. They're public, everyone uses them, and everyone benefits from them. But they can become clogged with overuse and unpleasant due to discourtesy. Follow the proper VHF protocol, and everyone will be in for a better boating experience — and a safer one, too.

[Excerpt 2 — CompleteGuideVHF.txt / 13	Bridge-to-bridge	Navigation, bridges, locks, commercial traffic]
MAYDAY signals grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. Use MAYDAY when lives are threatened, a vessel is sinking, someone has a medical emergency, or fire is out of control. MAYDAY calls get absolute priority on the radio.

To make a MAYDAY call, tune to Channel 16, set your radio to high power, and transmit: “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY. This is [vessel name], [vessel name], [vessel name].” Then provide your MMSI number if you have one, your position using latitude and longitude or bearing and distance from a known point, the nature of your distress, the kind of assistance you need, and the number of people on board.

Continue calling MAYDAY until you get a response. If you have a DSC-equipped radio, press the distress button to automatically alert the Coast Guard with your position and vessel information.

[Excerpt 3 — GMDSS VHF DSC procedures for small boat users - GOV.UK.pdf / Distress alert acknowledgement]
When a DSC radio receives a distress alert it will sound an audible alarm. Immediately cease any transmission that may interfere with distress traffic and continue a listening watch on Channel 16. If there is no DSC acknowledgement after a short interval (5 minutes) then, if you are able to offer assistance, acknowledge by voice on Channel 16: “Mayday “Name of vessel sending the distress message, followed by their call sign or MMSI “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]; Call sign or MMSI of your vessel “Received mayday “State what assistance you can give [including estimated time of arrival (ETA) if proceeding to the casualty] “Over” You should use any available means to relay the distress message to an appropriate coast station. Urgency If you are concerned about the safety of a person or vessel, you can send an urgency announcement using a DSC All Ships Urgency Call, nominating a working channel. Tune to Channel 16 to make the urgency call: “Pan pan, pan pan, pan pan “All stations – say 3 times. “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times] “Call sign or other identification “MMSI of own vessel “Please go to Channel [nominated working channel] “Out” Tune to the working channel and send your urgency message. Safety To pass safety information to HM Coastguard (HMCG) use an Individual DSC call with safety priority if available on your radio, entering the appropriate MMSI number. Transmit the DSC call and wait for the Coastguard acknowledgement. Accept the acknowledgement and ensure your radio is on the working channel indicated in the response. You should wait for the Coastguard to contact you on that channel. If your radio does not support the call, then you should make a voice call on Channel 16.

[Excerpt 1 — BoatUS.txt / 3 Tips for Using a VHF Radio]
In an emergency, your broadcast needs to be more structured. With the radio tuned to Channel 16 and the power set to high, begin your broadcast by stating either "Mayday" or "Pan-pan" three times over. Mayday is used when you're in a life-threatening situation. Pan-pan is the appropriate call to make when you're in a bad situation that isn't life threatening at the moment but could become life threatening. Next, state your vessel's name, latitude and longitude, a brief description of your boat, and the nature of your emergency. Speak slowly and clearly, and wait for a response from the Coast Guard. Once the Coast Guard knows the exact situation and location, be ready for some follow-up questions. You're likely to be asked about such things as the size and type of the boat you're on, the number and age of the people on board, and whether anyone has any medical training, if it's applicable to the situation.

Tip
Listen to make sure that the channel is clear before transmitting.
Even if you don't get an answer, continue making the emergency broadcast with those first three vital bits of information. The authorities (or perhaps a nearby pleasure boater) may be listening, even if you can't hear them calling back. Usually the best way to make sure your vital info gets through with no confusion or mistakes is to ensure that you have digital selective calling (DSC) active on your radio. This requires a Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number and a link to your GPS, unless you've got a newer VHF with a built-in GPS. When you press the DSC "panic button" on the VHF, the radio will automatically transmit your vessel information and exact location. And since it's digitally processed and uses narrow receiver bandwidth, it also boosts range over normal voice communications.

If you know for a fact that you haven't activated DSC, check out the article "Setting Up A VHF Radio With Digital Selective Calling", which tells you how to integrate your VHF and GPS. Then visit the MMSI website (free for members) to get an MMSI number and register your radio.

Think of VHF communications like the highways and byways of our nation. They're public, everyone uses them, and everyone benefits from them. But they can become clogged with overuse and unpleasant due to discourtesy. Follow the proper VHF protocol, and everyone will be in for a better boating experience — and a safer one, too.

How Do You Call A Coast Guard On VHF?
Try to remain calm
Turn your radio channel to 16
Say “coast guard” three times, followed by “this is” and the name of your vessel
State your location
State your emergency
Describe your needs
📢: The Coast Guard can only be contacted in an emergency or urgent situation.

How Do I Make A VHF Call?
1️⃣ Switch on the VHF unit and adjust the “squelch” until there is no more static

2️⃣ Do a radio check, but not on emergency channels. “open channels” such as 68, 69, and 72 can be used for radio checks.

3️⃣ Repeat “radio check” three times, followed by the name and location of your vessel.

4️⃣ Await confirmation from another station that your call has been heard and that your VHF radio is in working order.

5️⃣ Proceed to use the correct channels and terminology to communicate your needs.

You can also check out the YouTube video posted by Sailing Vagabond Epicurean featuring an interview with a US Coast Guard outlining basic procedures and information.

What Is A Push-To-Talk System?
Push-to-talk communication refers to a system whereby a button needs to be pushed to switch between voice reception and voice transmissions. This is a two-way communication mode, but only one person may speak at a time.

When a DSC radio receives a distress alert it will sound an audible alarm. Immediately cease any transmission that may interfere with distress traffic and continue a listening watch on Channel 16. If there is no DSC acknowledgement after a short interval (5 minutes) then, if you are able to offer assistance, acknowledge by voice on Channel 16: “Mayday “Name of vessel sending the distress message, followed by their call sign or MMSI “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]; Call sign or MMSI of your vessel “Received mayday “State what assistance you can give [including estimated time of arrival (ETA) if proceeding to the casualty] “Over” You should use any available means to relay the distress message to an appropriate coast station. When a DSC radio receives a distress alert it will sound an audible alarm. Immediately cease any transmission that may interfere with distress traffic and continue a listening watch on Channel 16. If there is no DSC acknowledgement after a short interval (5 minutes) then, if you are able to offer assistance, acknowledge by voice on Channel 16: “Mayday “Name of vessel sending the distress message, followed by their call sign or MMSI “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]; Call sign or MMSI of your vessel “Received mayday “State what assistance you can give [including estimated time of arrival (ETA) if proceeding to the casualty] “Over” You should use any available means to relay the distress message to an appropriate coast station. Urgency If you are concerned about the safety of a person or vessel, you can send an urgency announcement using a DSC All Ships Urgency Call, nominating a working channel. Tune to Channel 16 to make the urgency call: “Pan pan, pan pan, pan pan “All stations – say 3 times. “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times] “Call sign or other identification “MMSI of own vessel “Please go to Channel [nominated working channel] “Out” Tune to the working channel and send your urgency message. Safety To pass safety information to HM Coastguard (HMCG) use an Individual DSC call with safety priority if available on your radio, entering the appropriate MMSI number. Transmit the DSC call and wait for the Coastguard acknowledgement. Accept the acknowledgement and ensure your radio is on the working channel indicated in the response. You should wait for the Coastguard to contact you on that channel. If your radio does not support the call, then you should make a voice call on Channel 16.

- **Maintain communication discipline**, even if other participants do not.
- **Use the ship's name and the traffic centre's own name** in a call, not abbreviations or private names.
- Traffic participants with a reporting obligation **report in on the relevant channel**. Reporting off again is not necessary, unless a mandatory report applies.
- Traffic controllers ensure that **traffic participants make traffic arrangements among themselves** via the traffic channels. They may also mediate in this.
- **Do not hold discussions** on traffic channels.
- Use only the **approved working languages: Dutch or English**. In English, preferably use the Standard Marine Communication Phrases (SMCP). In an emergency, deviation from this is permitted.
- Use **message markers** (in both Dutch and English) to make clear the type of message.

[Excerpt 3 — BoatUS.txt / 3 Tips for Using a VHF Radio]
In an emergency, your broadcast needs to be more structured. With the radio tuned to Channel 16 and the power set to high, begin your broadcast by stating either "Mayday" or "Pan-pan" three times over. Mayday is used when you're in a life-threatening situation. Pan-pan is the appropriate call to make when you're in a bad situation that isn't life threatening at the moment but could become life threatening. Next, state your vessel's name, latitude and longitude, a brief description of your boat, and the nature of your emergency. Speak slowly and clearly, and wait for a response from the Coast Guard. Once the Coast Guard knows the exact situation and location, be ready for some follow-up questions. You're likely to be asked about such things as the size and type of the boat you're on, the number and age of the people on board, and whether anyone has any medical training, if it's applicable to the situation.

Tip
Listen to make sure that the channel is clear before transmitting.
Even if you don't get an answer, continue making the emergency broadcast with those first three vital bits of information. The authorities (or perhaps a nearby pleasure boater) may be listening, even if you can't hear them calling back. Usually the best way to make sure your vital info gets through with no confusion or mistakes is to ensure that you have digital selective calling (DSC) active on your radio. This requires a Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number and a link to your GPS, unless you've got a newer VHF with a built-in GPS. When you press the DSC "panic button" on the VHF, the radio will automatically transmit your vessel information and exact location. And since it's digitally processed and uses narrow receiver bandwidth, it also boosts range over normal voice communications.

If you know for a fact that you haven't activated DSC, check out the article "Setting Up A VHF Radio With Digital Selective Calling", which tells you how to integrate your VHF and GPS. Then visit the MMSI website (free for members) to get an MMSI number and register your radio.

Think of VHF communications like the highways and byways of our nation. They're public, everyone uses them, and everyone benefits from them. But they can become clogged with overuse and unpleasant due to discourtesy. Follow the proper VHF protocol, and everyone will be in for a better boating experience — and a safer one, too.

When a DSC radio receives a distress alert it will sound an audible alarm. Immediately cease any transmission that may interfere with distress traffic and continue a listening watch on Channel 16. If there is no DSC acknowledgement after a short interval (5 minutes) then, if you are able to offer assistance, acknowledge by voice on Channel 16: “Mayday “Name of vessel sending the distress message, followed by their call sign or MMSI “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]; Call sign or MMSI of your vessel “Received mayday “State what assistance you can give [including estimated time of arrival (ETA) if proceeding to the casualty] “Over” You should use any available means to relay the distress message to an appropriate coast station. Urgency If you are concerned about the safety of a person or vessel, you can send an urgency announcement using a DSC All Ships Urgency Call, nominating a working channel. Tune to Channel 16 to make the urgency call: “Pan pan, pan pan, pan pan “All stations – say 3 times. “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times] “Call sign or other identification “MMSI of own vessel “Please go to Channel [nominated working channel] “Out” Tune to the working channel and send your urgency message. Safety To pass safety information to HM Coastguard (HMCG) use an Individual DSC call with safety priority if available on your radio, entering the appropriate MMSI number. Transmit the DSC call and wait for the Coastguard acknowledgement. Accept the acknowledgement and ensure your radio is on the working channel indicated in the response. You should wait for the Coastguard to contact you on that channel. If your radio does not support the call, then you should make a voice call on Channel 16.

Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

Modern VHF radios include Digital Selective Calling, a technology that transforms marine safety. DSC radios can send distress alerts with the press of one button, automatically including your vessel information and GPS position. Understanding these features adds a powerful safety layer to your boating.

What Is Digital Selective Calling?
DSC adds digital messaging capability to standard voice VHF radios. Instead of broadcasting to everyone on a channel, DSC lets you send digital messages to specific vessels or shore stations. The most important DSC feature is the distress button, typically protected by a flip-cover to prevent accidental activation.

When you press the DSC distress button, your radio automatically sends an alert on Channel 70 (the dedicated DSC data channel) containing your MMSI number, vessel information, and GPS coordinates if connected. The Coast Guard receives this alert within seconds and can respond immediately knowing exactly where you are.

MAYDAY signals grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. Use MAYDAY when lives are threatened, a vessel is sinking, someone has a medical emergency, or fire is out of control. MAYDAY calls get absolute priority on the radio.

To make a MAYDAY call, tune to Channel 16, set your radio to high power, and transmit: “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY. This is [vessel name], [vessel name], [vessel name].” Then provide your MMSI number if you have one, your position using latitude and longitude or bearing and distance from a known point, the nature of your distress, the kind of assistance you need, and the number of people on board.

Continue calling MAYDAY until you get a response. If you have a DSC-equipped radio, press the distress button to automatically alert the Coast Guard with your position and vessel information.

[Excerpt 2 — IMO standard marine comms phrases.pdf / NAV 46/WP.3]
Upon receipt of a DSC Distress Alert acknowledgement the vessel in distress should commence the distress traffic on one of the international distress traffic frequencies for telephony (VHF Channel 16 or 2182 kHz) as follows: MAYDAY THIS IS - the 9-digit Maritime Mobile Service Identity code (MMSI) plus name / call sign or other identification of the vessel calling - the position of the vessel - the nature of distress - the assistance required - any other information which might facilitate rescue.

[SECTION BREAK]

MAYDAY

[Excerpt 3 — BoatUS.txt / 3 Tips for Using a VHF Radio]
In an emergency, your broadcast needs to be more structured. With the radio tuned to Channel 16 and the power set to high, begin your broadcast by stating either "Mayday" or "Pan-pan" three times over. Mayday is used when you're in a life-threatening situation. Pan-pan is the appropriate call to make when you're in a bad situation that isn't life threatening at the moment but could become life threatening. Next, state your vessel's name, latitude and longitude, a brief description of your boat, and the nature of your emergency. Speak slowly and clearly, and wait for a response from the Coast Guard. Once the Coast Guard knows the exact situation and location, be ready for some follow-up questions. You're likely to be asked about such things as the size and type of the boat you're on, the number and age of the people on board, and whether anyone has any medical training, if it's applicable to the situation.

Tip
Listen to make sure that the channel is clear before transmitting.
Even if you don't get an answer, continue making the emergency broadcast with those first three vital bits of information. The authorities (or perhaps a nearby pleasure boater) may be listening, even if you can't hear them calling back. Usually the best way to make sure your vital info gets through with no confusion or mistakes is to ensure that you have digital selective calling (DSC) active on your radio. This requires a Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number and a link to your GPS, unless you've got a newer VHF with a built-in GPS. When you press the DSC "panic button" on the VHF, the radio will automatically transmit your vessel information and exact location. And since it's digitally processed and uses narrow receiver bandwidth, it also boosts range over normal voice communications.

If you know for a fact that you haven't activated DSC, check out the article "Setting Up A VHF Radio With Digital Selective Calling", which tells you how to integrate your VHF and GPS. Then visit the MMSI website (free for members) to get an MMSI number and register your radio.

Think of VHF communications like the highways and byways of our nation. They're public, everyone uses them, and everyone benefits from them. But they can become clogged with overuse and unpleasant due to discourtesy. Follow the proper VHF protocol, and everyone will be in for a better boating experience — and a safer one, too.

What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Conclusion
Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Unlike cell phones that fail when you need them most, a properly operated VHF radio connects you to rescue services, other boaters, and essential information anywhere your boat can reach. The skills covered in this guide, from basic operation to emergency procedures, become automatic with practice.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

[Excerpt 3 — BoatUS.txt / boatus]
Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Conclusion
Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Unlike cell phones that fail when you need them most, a properly operated VHF radio connects you to rescue services, other boaters, and essential information anywhere your boat can reach. The skills covered in this guide, from basic operation to emergency procedures, become automatic with practice.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

[Excerpt 1 — BoatUS.txt / boatus]
Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Conclusion
Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Unlike cell phones that fail when you need them most, a properly operated VHF radio connects you to rescue services, other boaters, and essential information anywhere your boat can reach. The skills covered in this guide, from basic operation to emergency procedures, become automatic with practice.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.
